summary:
North Carolina lies within the United States, and the federal layer governes the sharpest exposures a trans visitor faces. Executive Order 14168, in force since January 2025, requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department has stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth, issues new passports only as M or F according to supporting documents, and leaves passports already issued with an X marker valid until expiry. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad; the ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.

Entry carries a second, distinct exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code SWS25. The same announcement states that an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently.

Checkpoint screening risks involuntary disclosure. The National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request a screening of the type matching one's presentation.

At state level, the national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 classifies North Carolina as moderate-risk, alongside Alaska and Kentucky, and places it below the national score of 0.36. Facility use in the state has been contested law before and remains an active legislative subject. House Bill 2, passed by the North Carolina General Assembly in emergency session after the Charlotte city council's March 2016 ordinance allowing transgender people to use bathrooms matching their gender identity, barred cities from passing anti-discrimination ordinances protecting gay and transgender people and required public bathroom use to correspond with the sex listed on a birth certificate. Legislators repealed House Bill 2 on 30 March 2017, but as of 25 March 2025 Republican lawmakers were again pushing a bathroom bill in the 2025 session.

Lethal risk is recorded separately from the legal tier. A national data analysis published 16 July 2026 places North Carolina at 3.0 killings per 100k trans women with three or more recorded victims, an acknowledged undercount, and characterises the state as moderate-risk; the same analysis finds that protective statutes do not predict lower lethal risk for trans women. North Carolina's recorded rate sits mid-pack among states with documented killings, so the post-2017 legal position does not by itself lower what a visitor can expect on the ground.
tangentialFactors:
Identity documents are the fastest-moving area of restriction across the United States. Kansas has enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not bear sex assigned at birth and barring trans residents from changing those markers, which rights groups describe as a template other legislatures are following, with further targeting bills pending. The Movement Advancement Project's identity-document map sets out state by state which jurisdictions permit gender-marker changes on licences and birth certificates and under what conditions, so the rules encountered depend heavily on the state involved.

Facility-use bans are widespread nationally. State bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one territory, with additional states imposing outright bans on facility use according to gender identity, and in some jurisdictions trans bathroom use is a criminal offence in certain circumstances. Twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. Enforcement is no longer theoretical: in April 2025 a trans student who announced 'I am here to break the law' and used a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol was arrested and handcuffed, which civil-rights attorneys identified as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.

Foreign governments have responded publicly to the federal document and data rules. At least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the United States, and those advisories followed detentions of European citizens over visa issues.

The 13 July 2026 national legal risk assessment identifies Idaho as the latest state flagged do-not-travel for trans people, bringing the total to four states so designated, and records that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights alongside the federal measures driving nationwide trends. North Carolina is not among the do-not-travel states.
